group.passage:
Imagine two tea bowls on a table. One is smooth, perfectly round, and painted with fine blue flowers. The other is dark and heavy, a little lopsided, with a rough surface and a small chip in its rim. Many people would reach for the first. A great Japanese tea master of the sixteenth century would almost certainly have chosen the second.
That preference has a name: wabi-sabi. Wabi describes a quiet, simple kind of beauty that does without decoration, while sabi refers to the charm that things gain as they grow old, the way a stone step wears smooth or metal takes on rust. Together the words point to a way of seeing that finds value in what is plain, aging, and imperfect. It is not, however, a love of poverty or gloom. Even the meal at a small tea gathering was meant to be modest rather than meager: one soup and two or three dishes.
The idea was written about long before anyone made tea bowls to express it. In 1332, the Buddhist priest Yoshida Kenko asked in an essay whether cherry blossoms are worth looking at only in full bloom, or the moon only on a cloudless night. To him, branches just about to flower, or a garden covered in fallen petals, were even more moving. Two centuries later, the tea master Sen no Rikyu brought this taste into everyday objects. Turning away from costly bowls brought in from China, he asked a local potter, Chojiro, to make simple earthenware bowls whose uneven shapes were partly left to the fire. A record of his teachings even says that anyone who rejects a piece because of slight damage has missed the point.
Nature can create the same effect without anyone planning it. When the garden of Saihoji temple in Kyoto was laid out in 1339, it was a scene of white sand and pine trees. Over the following centuries, especially after the temple fell into neglect, moss slowly spread across the grounds. Today more than 120 kinds cover them, and the place is known simply as the moss temple. Its gardeners now sweep as little as possible in winter so as not to disturb the resting moss.

translation_zh.text:
想像桌上放著兩個茶碗。一個光滑、渾圓，畫著細緻的藍色花朵；另一個顏色暗沉、沉甸甸的，有點歪，表面粗糙，碗口還有一個小缺角。很多人會伸手拿第一個；但一位十六世紀的日本茶道大師，幾乎一定會選第二個。
這種偏好有個名字：侘寂（wabi-sabi）。「侘」指一種安靜、簡單、不需要裝飾的美；「寂」則指事物隨著歲月變老而產生的韻味，就像石階被磨得光滑、金屬生了鏽。兩個字合起來，指的是一種在樸素、老去、不完美的事物中看見價值的眼光。不過，它並不是喜愛貧窮或陰鬱。即使是小型茶會的餐點，也講求簡樸而不寒酸：一湯配兩三道菜。
早在有人做出茶碗來表現這種想法之前，它就已經被寫進文章裡。1332 年，佛教僧人吉田兼好在一篇文章中問道：櫻花只有在盛開時才值得看嗎？月亮只有在無雲的夜晚才值得看嗎？對他來說，含苞待放的枝頭，或落滿花瓣的庭院，更加動人。兩百年後，茶道大師千利休把這種品味帶進日常器物。他捨棄從中國進口的昂貴茶碗，請本地陶工長次郎製作簡樸的土碗，碗的不規則形狀有一部分交給窯火決定。一份記錄他教誨的文獻甚至說，凡是因為一點小損傷就嫌棄器物的人，都沒有抓到重點。
大自然不需要任何人計畫，也能造出同樣的效果。京都西芳寺的庭園在 1339 年建造時，是一片白沙與松樹的景色。在之後的幾百年間，尤其是寺院荒廢之後，苔蘚慢慢長滿了整個庭園。如今這裡有超過 120 種苔蘚，人們乾脆稱它為「苔寺」。現在園丁冬天盡量少打掃，以免打擾正在休眠的苔蘚。

open_tasks.prompt: Think of an old or imperfect object you own or have seen. In 1–2 English sentences, explain how someone who values wabi-sabi might see it.
reference_answers: My grandmother’s wooden table has scratches from years of use, and someone who values wabi-sabi would see those marks as part of its beauty and history.
A cup with a small chip might look damaged to most people, but a wabi-sabi view would value its simple shape and the signs that it has been used for a long time.
